summary: This standards-track document defines an Interactive Voice Response package for the Media Control Channel Framework. It specifies requests to prepare, start, and stop dialog interactions on media connections and conferences, along with responses and notifications. The dialogs themselves are in a separate dialog language.

plainLanguage.summary: When you call a company and a voice says press one for sales, someone's program controls it. This defines the commands for starting and stopping that menu.

questions: how to control ivr dialogs on media server
what is the mediactrl ivr control package
how does a media server play prompts and collect dtmf
subtitle: How an application server tells a media server to play prompts, collect keypresses and record callers.

tldr.problem: Applications that run voice menus and announcements need a standard way to tell a remote media server what to play, collect and record on a call or conference.
tldr.mechanism: The package defines XML elements carried over the Media Control Channel Framework to prepare, start and terminate dialogs, plus responses, notifications and audit requests. It includes a lightweight dialog language for prompts, runtime controls, DTMF collection and recording, and allows other languages such as VoiceXML by reference.
tldr.outcome: A Proposed Standard published in May 2011 with the control package name msc-ivr/1.0. It is updated by RFC 6623.

today: RFC 6231 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2011 and is updated by RFC 6623. It has not been obsoleted by a later RFC.

sections.title: An IVR Package for the Control Framework
sections.content:
The Media Control Channel Framework (RFC 6230) lets an application server (AS) send commands to a media server (MS) over a reliable channel set up with SIP. A control package is a specific use of that framework. This RFC defines the package for Interactive Voice Response (IVR) dialogs on media connections and conferences. Here a 'dialog' means an IVR dialog and has nothing to do with a SIP dialog.

The package name is msc-ivr/1.0, and it is registered with IANA together with the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:msc-ivr and the MIME type application/msc-ivr+xml. It is designed to meet the IVR requirements in RFC 5167, and borrows ideas from earlier SIP media server languages and from W3C voice browser languages.

Out of scope for the built-in dialog language are speech recognition, text-to-speech, fax, automatic prompt recovery and media transformation. Those can come from other dialog languages, from extensions in other XML namespaces, or from other control packages.

The MS acts as the Control Server, receiving requests from the AS (the Control Client). It also acts as a Control Client when it sends event notifications. Everything sits inside a root <mscivr> element whose version attribute is fixed at 1.0. Requests and notifications travel in CONTROL messages, and responses in a 200 response or REPORT messages. The MS MUST support HTTP and HTTPS for fetching and uploading resources.
sections.plainLanguage: A computer program in charge of a phone menu sends short typed instructions to a machine that makes the sounds. This document says exactly how those instructions look.

sections.title: Preparing, Starting and Ending Dialogs
sections.content:
Three requests manage a dialog. <dialogprepare> fetches and validates a dialog and any resources it references, without running it. <dialogstart> runs a dialog on a connection or a conference, preparing it first if needed. <dialogterminate> stops one. A start request names exactly one of connectionid or conferenceid; naming both or neither is a syntax error (400).

The dialog itself is given in exactly one of three ways: inline as a <dialog> element, as an external document by the src attribute, or as a previously prepared dialog by prepareddialogid. The MS MUST support the inline IVR dialog language and MAY support other languages by reference. A <stream> element can restrict which media streams a dialog uses and in which direction.

Every request gets a <response> with a numeric status and a dialogid. A <subscribe> element asks for DTMF notifications, and the MS reports them with <dtmfnotify>. When a dialog ends for any reason, the MS MUST send a <dialogexit> event. <dialogterminate> takes an immediate attribute, default false: when false, the dialog finishes its current iteration and the exit event carries report information.
sections.plainLanguage: You can get a recording ready ahead of time, press play when a caller is on the line, or stop it. The machine always answers 'done' or 'could not do it', and tells you when the recording is over.

sections.title: The Dialog Lifecycle
sections.content:
The MS MUST follow a fixed lifecycle. A dialog starts in IDLE, moves through PREPARING and PREPARED or straight through STARTING to STARTED, and ends in TERMINATED. Once TERMINATED, its identifier is no longer valid and can be reused, and no notifications may be sent for it.

A prepared dialog that waits too long is dropped: if it stays PREPARED beyond the maximum preparation duration, it is terminated and the MS sends a dialogexit with an error status. A maximum of 300s is RECOMMENDED. If a dialog is terminated while still being prepared or started, the original request gets a 410 response.

The status in <dialogexit> tells the AS why the dialog ended. An AS MUST treat any code it does not recognize as 4, a dialog execution error.
sections.plainLanguage: A dialog is like a toy on a shelf. It is put on the shelf (prepared), played with (started), and put away (terminated). Once it is put away, you cannot play with that same toy again.

sections.title: The IVR Dialog Language
sections.content:
The built-in language has a <dialog> container with up to four kinds of child: <prompt> plays media in order (<media>, <variable> for dates, times and digits, <dtmf> tones, and <par> for parallel playback), <control> maps keys to runtime controls, <collect> gathers DTMF digits, and <record> records the caller. A dialog can repeat using repeatCount, repeatDur and repeatUntilComplete.

With a prompt and bargein enabled (the default), keypresses stop the prompt and start collection or recording. The runtime controls are keys for fast forward, rewind, pause, resume, volume and speed, such as ffkey and pausekey. They are active only while a prompt plays. For collection, the defaults include a 5s initial timeout, a 2s inter-digit timeout, maxdigits of 5 and a termination character of '#'. A custom grammar can replace them, and the MS MUST support SRGS XML grammars. Recording has a default maxtime of 15s and can use voice activity detection to start or stop.

When a dialog ends normally, the exit event reports results in <promptinfo>, <controlinfo>, <collectinfo> and <recordinfo>, each with a termmode that says how that step finished. The package does not specify which media formats or codecs an MS supports.
sections.plainLanguage: A dialog is a little script: say something, listen for button presses, or record what the caller says. It can also let callers pause, rewind or turn the volume up while a message plays.

sections.title: Auditing a Media Server
sections.content:
The <audit> request lets the AS ask what the MS can do and which dialogs it is running. The capabilities and dialogs attributes both default to true, and dialogid narrows the dialog audit to one dialog (an invalid identifier gets a 406). The MS MUST reply with an <auditresponse>.

Capability data covers supported codecs, dialog languages, grammar types, record types, prompt types and variable types, and the maximum prepared and record durations. The RFC gives two uses: discovering capabilities before starting a dialog, including choosing codecs for the SDP of a user agent's connection, and letting one AS take over dialogs when the AS that started them fails or is no longer available.
sections.plainLanguage: Before giving the sound machine a job, you can ask it what tricks it knows and what it is busy doing right now.

sections.title: Response Status Codes
sections.content:
The package uses its own numeric status codes in <response> and <auditresponse>. 200 means success. The 4xx codes fall in three groups: a syntax error in the request (400), an error executing the request on the MS (405 to 419), and a request that needs a capability the MS does not support (420 to 439). An AS MUST treat an unrecognized code as the x00 code of its class, so an unknown 499 is read as 400.

The AS SHOULD NOT retry the same request unchanged, though the same request to a different MS might succeed if that MS has the needed capability. The MS SHOULD use the most specific code available, and the reason attribute should explain the failure in more detail.
sections.plainLanguage: If the machine cannot do what you asked, it says why with a number: your note was written wrong, something went wrong while doing it, or it simply does not know that trick.

sections.title: Using VoiceXML as a Dialog Language
sections.content:
The package allows, but does not require, other dialog languages by reference. Section 9 is normative for an MS that supports VoiceXML. The AS sets type to application/voicexml+xml and src to the document URI in <dialogprepare> or <dialogstart>. The MS MUST support the fetchtimeout attribute in its VoiceXML environment.

When it starts a VoiceXML dialog, the MS MUST map connection, media stream and parameter information into VoiceXML session variables, for example the SIP URIs of the call and the values in <params>. <dtmfsub> subscriptions are not defined for VoiceXML, so asking for one gets a 439 response.
sections.plainLanguage: If the machine speaks a fancier scripting language, you can hand it a script written in that language, and it will pass along the facts about the call so the script knows who is calling.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations MUST address the security of the control channel as described in RFC 6230, of the user agent sessions, and of any HTTP-style fetches and uploads. The RFC lists attacks if this is done badly: denial of service by injecting <dialogterminate immediate='true'> for a guessed dialog identifier, resource exhaustion with a very long fetchtimeout and a bogus URL, phishing by changing a <media> loc to a different audio file, and data theft by adding a second recording location to a <record>.

The package adds channel rules. The MS MUST send responses and notifications only on the control channel that created the dialog, and MUST only provide audit information for dialogs created on the same channel. It SHOULD reject audit or manipulation requests from another channel with a framework 403 response. The RFC allows exceptions, such as an administrator channel or taking over dialogs after an AS failure, but says their implications must be weighed carefully.
sections.plainLanguage: If a stranger could slip fake orders into the line, they could hang up calls, swap the recorded message, or copy what callers say. So the line must be locked, and only the boss who started a job can change it.

items.label: Terminated
items.desc: The dialog was ended by a dialogterminate request.

items.label: Connection gone
items.desc: The connection or conference associated with the dialog terminated.

items.label: Too long
items.desc: The dialog exceeded its maximum duration.

items.label: Execution error
items.desc: An error occurred while the dialog ran.

viz.caption: THREE COMMON DIALOG MODELS IN THE DIALOG ELEMENT

items.title: playannouncements
items.text: Only a prompt; its media resources play in sequence.

items.title: promptandcollect
items.text: A collect element, optionally with a prompt; DTMF collection starts after the prompt or on bargein.

items.title: promptandrecord
items.text: A record element, optionally with a prompt; recording starts after the prompt or on bargein.

items.label: Syntax error
items.desc: The request is not valid against the schema or breaks a co-occurrence rule.

items.label: dialogid already exists
items.desc: The dialog identifier is already used by another dialog on the MS.

items.label: dialogid does not exist
items.desc: The dialog identifier names no dialog on the MS.

items.label: connectionid does not exist
items.desc: The connection is not available on the MS.

items.label: conferenceid does not exist
items.desc: The conference is not available on the MS.

items.label: Resource cannot be retrieved
items.desc: An external dialog, media or grammar could not be fetched within the timeout.

items.label: Dialog execution canceled
items.desc: A dialogterminate request ended a dialog being prepared or started.

items.label: Unsupported URI scheme
items.desc: The MS does not support the scheme of a URI in the request.

items.label: Unsupported dialog language
items.desc: The request references a dialog language the MS does not support.
